English biology Borrowed from New Latin biologia (1766), itself from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “bio-, life”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”). By surface analysis, bio- + -logy.

senses.d: The study of all life or living matter.
ex: Near-synonyms: life science, life sciences; see also Thesaurus:biology

senses.d: The living organisms of a particular region.
The structure, function, and behavior of an organism or type of organism.

ety.text: As a French word, coined by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1802. Possibly formed as bio- + -logie. Possibly borrowed from German Biologie or New Latin biologia. In any case, derived from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “bio-, life”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy, branch of study, to speak”).
From bio- + -logia. Piecewise doublet of zoologia.

From bio- + -logía, from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos, “life”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation, narrative”) + -ία (-ía), elements used to coin analogous terms in different languages c. 1800. See English biology for more information.
Borrowed from French biologie, from German Biologie or New Latin biologia. By surface analysis, bio- + -logia. Piecewise doublet of zoologia.

senses.d: A person's life story, especially one published.
ex: There are many biographies of Benjamin Franklin.

senses.d: The art of writing this kind of story.
ex: She is best known for biography and history, but she is also a novelist.
